title: {{NAME}} and the Tournament of the Golden Crown
moral: A true champion lifts the whole team, because a victory shared is worth a hundred won alone.

pages.content:
The Royal Tournament Grounds were the kind of place that made you stand straighter just by looking at them. Banners in a hundred kingdom colours snapped in a warm, perfumed wind. The pitch itself was a carpet of grass so perfectly, improbably green it seemed to be showing off. And the goalposts at each end were gold, real gold, bright as noon sunlight, hung with garlands of fresh flowers.

{{NAME}} had found the entrance by following a trail of golden footprints that appeared and vanished on the cobblestones of the old town, leading him through an archway that smelled of orange blossom and fresh turf. On the other side: this.

Teams from a dozen kingdoms were warming up on the far pitches. Knights, apprentices, young nobles in their kingdom colours, all moving with the focused grace of people who had trained seriously. And in the centre of it all, a referee in a silver cloak was pinning a small, crimson team badge onto a notice board with the name: THE WANDERERS. Below it, a single name slot was still empty.

pages.content:
The Wanderers were three players, and they were extraordinary.

Princess Isolde was their captain and centre-forward, tall for her age with close-cropped hair and the kind of absolute composure that suggested she had played in front of crowds that could roar like oceans. She moved with the long, unhurried grace of someone who always knew exactly where the ball was going to be.

Beside her was Finn, a quick, clever midfielder with freckles and a way of vanishing between defenders that seemed physically improbable. And sweeper was a stocky, grinning girl called Petra, who stopped shots the way a mountain stops weather.

They needed a fourth. And somehow, inexplicably, the silver-cloaked referee was looking at {{NAME}}.

"You're listed," the referee said simply, in a tone that did not invite argument.

Isolde studied {{NAME}} with cool, serious eyes. "Right winger," she said. "You cross, I finish. Can you deliver an accurate ball under pressure?"

{{NAME}} took a breath. He could. He absolutely could. "Yes," he said.

pages.content:
The semi-final was against the Irongate Strikers, a team from a northern mountain kingdom who played with the grinding, physical efficiency of a millstone. They didn't do elegant. They did relentless.

For forty minutes, the Wanderers matched them move for move. Petra was magnificent, blocking with her whole body, throwing herself sideways with a grin that refused to falter. Finn slipped through gaps that didn't exist. Isolde was a constant threat, her composure maddening to the Irongate defenders, who couldn't rattle her no matter how hard they tried.

With three minutes left, {{NAME}} received the ball on the right wing. Two defenders converged. The ground felt solid under his white boots. He looked up once, fast, and saw Isolde making her run, perfectly timed, a red blur against the golden midday light.

The Irongate goalkeeper had positioned for a near-post shot. {{NAME}} knew it instantly. He curved the cross high and far, bending it on an arc that landed precisely, impossibly, exactly where Isolde's head arrived a half-second later.

The ball hit the back of the net with a sound like a silk flag snapping in a gale.

pages.content:
The final was against the Crystal Palace team, the defending champions, and they were, by any measure, spectacular. Their captain was a princess named Aurelia, whose passing was so precise it looked like geometry and whose smile before a match suggested she had already seen the result.

The Wanderers were one goal down with seven minutes to go.

Isolde called them together. Her composure, for the first time all tournament, had a fracture in it. Not panic, but something human and honest. "I can't get past their back line," she admitted.

The four of them stood in a tight circle. Petra spoke first. "Finn, go deeper, pull the sweeper." Finn nodded. {{NAME}} added, "If you draw the sweeper, there's space in behind on the left for Isolde." Isolde's eyes sharpened. "And if their keeper commits early?" "She will," {{NAME}} said quietly. "She's done it on every set piece."

Isolde looked at him with an expression that was not quite a smile but was something better. "Then let's make a set piece happen."

They did. The net rippled. Then again, in the final minute. The Golden Crown was theirs.

pages.content:
The Golden Crown trophy was smaller than {{NAME}} had imagined, a delicate thing of real gold in the shape of interlocking leaves, catching the late afternoon light like a small captured sun.

Isolde lifted it, then immediately passed it to Petra, who passed it to Finn, who held it out to {{NAME}} with both hands. The crowd around the golden goalposts was making a sound like the sea.

Petra slung a mud-caked arm around {{NAME}}'s shoulders. "That was the best cross I have seen," she said matter-of-factly, "in my entire life."

The orange-blossom archway was waiting at the edge of the grounds when the sky began to turn amber. {{NAME}} stepped back through it, the golden afternoon light of the ordinary town warm on his face.

He was in his bed early that night, pleasantly, thoroughly tired, his boots by the door still faintly green at the toe. The small gold crown emblem on his jersey caught the lamplight as his eyes closed.

He was nearly asleep when he remembered: Isolde had pressed a folded note into his hand at the gate. He hadn't opened it yet.
